Cairngorms by Motorcycle: Scotland's Mountain Heart

The Cairngorms National Park is Britain's largest national park, covering 1,748 square miles of mountain, forest, and river valley in the Scottish Highlands. For motorcyclists, it offers a compelling mix of fast flowing A-roads, quiet forest roads through ancient Caledonian pine, and mountain passes with vast panoramas.

Key Roads

  • A93 Braemar to Glenshee: Scotland's highest public road, climbing over the Cairnwell Pass at 670m (2,199ft). The ski area at the summit is bleak but atmospheric, and the road itself is fast and flowing.
  • B970 Kingussie to Coylumbridge: A quieter alternative to the A9, passing through Glen Feshie and the ancient pine forests around Inshriach. Beautiful, quiet riding.
  • A939 Tomintoul to Cock Bridge (the Lecht): A dramatic mountain road often closed in winter. The highest section crosses exposed moorland at 635m. In summer, it's a superb ride.
  • B974 Cairn o' Mount: A historic route over the Mounth between Deeside and the coast. The summit panorama across the eastern Highlands is vast.

Forest Roads

The Cairngorms contain the largest remaining areas of ancient Caledonian pine forest in Scotland:

  • Rothiemurchus Forest: The road from Aviemore to Loch Morlich passes through magnificent old-growth pine. Red squirrels, crested tits, and Scottish crossbills inhabit these woods.
  • Abernethy Forest: Near Nethybridge. RSPB reserve with osprey and capercaillie. The forest roads are atmospheric.
  • Glen Tanar: On Deeside near Aboyne. Ancient pine and birch woodland along the Water of Tanar.

Whisky Country

The eastern edge of the Cairngorms is Speyside — the heart of Scotch whisky production. Distilleries line the River Spey:

  • Aberlour, Glenfiddich, Macallan, Glenlivet, Cardhu — all offer tours
  • The Malt Whisky Trail connects seven distilleries in a signposted route
  • Driver/rider: enjoy tours but save tasting for the evening
The Cairngorms have some of the most extreme weather in Britain. The mountain passes can be snow-covered into May and blizzards can occur even in June. Check mountain weather forecasts (MWIS) before riding the high passes, and be prepared for temperatures 10-15°C below the valley floor.

Wildlife and Nature

The Cairngorms are one of the best areas in Britain for wildlife. Red deer are common and visible from the road, especially at dawn and dusk. Ospreys nest at Loch Garten — the RSPB visitor centre has live camera feeds and viewing telescopes. Red squirrels are abundant in the pine forests, particularly around Rothiemurchus and Abernethy.

The Cairngorm Mountain itself has a funicular railway to the summit plateau at 1,097m. The views from the top on a clear day extend across the entire Highland range. The mountain centre at the top has a café and exhibition, though walkers are asked not to descend beyond the viewing terrace unless properly equipped.

Aviemore, the main town in the Cairngorms, has all necessary facilities including fuel, accommodation, restaurants, and outdoor equipment shops. It makes an excellent base for multi-day touring, with different riding routes available in every direction from the town. keyTakeaways: The Cairngorms National Park is Britain's largest, covering 1,748 square miles of mountain, forest and river valley.
The A93 over the Cairnwell Pass at 670m (2,199ft) is Scotland's highest public road, fast and flowing.
The A939 to the Lecht and the B974 Cairn o' Mount deliver dramatic mountain passes, often closed in winter.
Rothiemurchus and Abernethy hold the largest ancient Caledonian pine forest, home to red squirrels and ospreys.
The eastern edge is Speyside whisky country; enjoy distillery tours but save tasting for the evening if riding.

faq.q: How high do the Cairngorms roads climb?
faq.a: The A93 over the Cairnwell Pass between Braemar and Glenshee reaches 670m (2,199ft), making it Scotland's highest public road. The A939 to the Lecht crosses exposed moorland at 635m, and the B974 Cairn o' Mount climbs to a summit with a vast panorama across the eastern Highlands. These high passes are fast and flowing in summer but demand respect for the altitude and weather.

faq.q: What is the weather like on the passes?
faq.a: The Cairngorms have some of the most extreme weather in Britain. The mountain passes can be snow-covered into May and blizzards can occur even in June. Check mountain weather forecasts such as MWIS before riding the high passes, and be prepared for temperatures 10 to 15 degrees below the valley floor. The A939 Lecht road and the A93 are often closed altogether in winter.

faq.q: Can I visit the whisky distilleries while riding?
faq.a: The eastern edge of the Cairngorms is Speyside, the heart of Scotch whisky production, with Aberlour, Glenfiddich, Macallan, Glenlivet and Cardhu all offering tours. The signposted Malt Whisky Trail connects seven distilleries. As a rider you can enjoy the tours, but save any tasting for the evening when you have finished riding for the day. Never sample and ride.

faq.q: What wildlife can I expect to see?
faq.a: The Cairngorms are one of the best areas in Britain for wildlife. Red deer are common and visible from the road, especially at dawn and dusk. Ospreys nest at Loch Garten, where the RSPB visitor centre has live camera feeds and telescopes. Red squirrels are abundant in the pine forests, particularly around Rothiemurchus and Abernethy, and capercaillie inhabit Abernethy Forest.
